doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Sadik Hakim, Stanley Crouch and the Tin Palace
summary: Hakim used LaLama on gigs; Crouch asked if he was white and wanted Junior Cook; it later worked out, and LaLama says he loves black music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Okay. I used to play with this guy named Sadik Hakim, which his real name was Argonne Thornton, he used to play with Bird. He was a kid when he played with Bird. He lived with Bird, he wasn’t that good, he was learning how to play. He wasn’t Bud Powell, but Bird let him play when Hakim did a record with Bird and Argonne now is grown up and I moved to New York and he befriended me. Okay? He was an older black guy, a great piano player at that time.

Sadik Hakim. Yeah. He’s dead. But he lived in the lower East side and, but he was a real jazzer man. He kind of played between, he had originals, he wrote thousands of tunes and he had a lot of originals that sounded like between Monk and Duke and Horace, you know those kinds of tunes. He wrote great tunes. And every time — he was pretty famous so he would do a lot of trio gigs. And he would have quartet gigs and he would use me, because I would go play with him a lot and I liked his tunes, so we got along, I guess he liked me. So one time there was a place called the Tin Palace. And Sadik got a gig there and then he was going to use me, and Stanley Crouch used to book him. And then he goes, Stanley said, “Who do you have in the group?” Uh bu-bu-bu “I have this tenor player you probably never heard of named Ralph LaLama.” “No I never heard of him. Is he white?” “Yeah.” Na, na, na, na, don’t get — get Junior Cook. Okay. So Sadik told me this. Okay? So I go to the Tin Palace and they were playing, and I brought my horn to sit in. See? And I love Junior Cook. I wasn’t trying to blow any — I couldn’t, because I was a kid. But anyway, to make a long story short, so I went there to play, and then Stan, and he said “this is Ralph LaLama.” Okay. And I could have got out on Stanley and I didn’t. Something told me no. Because Stanley I knew, he’s a writer, I like Stanley actually, but at that time I didn’t really like him too much. Okay. Now, now, now he wrote, I’ll forward to about ten years later, and now I’m on the scene more you know. And Stanley comes down to the Vanguard, he knows who I am, so he wrote an article in the Village Voice called “The Tell of the Tenor,” you know in other words talking about the backstory, from Chu Berry until now, at that time, probably about twelve or fifteen years ago. But it was ten years later after the scene at the Tin Palace. And to make a long story short, he was talking about Lester Young, Coltrane, Sonny Rollins, all the great tenor players, and then at the end he started talking about now we’ve got guys like ba-ba-ba we’ve got this guy, we’ve got this guy, and Joshua Redman, and then the three Caucasian tenor players that I like who are on the New York scene is Ralph LaLama, Joe Lovano and Mike Brecker. I said yes. So I mean because I had a little restraint. Because see it © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

didn’t bother me because of the way I grew up. That’s why I didn’t mean to tell you this long story but you asked the question and I had a history with it. I never thought that way because I know it’s black music, that’s why I like it. You know, because to me this music is killing. I really don’t like white music, to tell you the truth. I’m serious. That’s what bothers me sometimes about rock & roll too, it’s just a little too Caucasian for me, and I’m just telling you the truth okay. That’s the way I grew up, what am I going to do? So anyway, so the point of it is that he wrote that so it all worked out you know what I mean? He wrote that thing about putting my name in the paper and put those guys, Lovano and Michael. That was great. So it worked out. But I guess in some people’s mind it does hinder you and in some people’s mind it helps you too, you know, I guess. Some people won’t hire you because you’re white I guess and some people will hire you because you’re white. But I have a lot of friends, I don’t really think of it that way. I know people do. But I don’t care. You know these guys are friends of mine. I don’t think about black or white. They’re friends. They’ve always been friends. And pre-grade school. I learned how to play sports, you know I could play sports too because of these guys, but I could play with the old guys. These guys would kick my butt you know. Does that answer your question?
Yeah that’s a good answer. That’s a good story.
